newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Tajik rebels still haggling over hostages.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Tajik rebels still haggling over hostages.

text.p: Russian Deputy Prime Minister Vitaly Ignatyenko pressed on with delicate negotiations with Tajik Islamist guerrillas on Saturday to secure the release of 11 hostages still being held by the rebels.
"I have just had a conversation with (rebel leader) Bakhram Sadirov. We are seeking a way for the exchange of the remaining hostages," Interfax news agency quoted Ignatyenko as saying.
"We have already achieved a good deal -- the release of three of the captives in exchange for six fighters," he added.

Late on Friday three hostages -- two Russian women reporters from Itar-Tass and Interfax news agencies and a driver -- were freed from the captors' base on a mountain top in a barren rocky region about 80 km (50 miles) from the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
"We're fine," Tass quoted its reporter, Galina Gridneva, as saying by telephone after her release.
Sadirov's rebels have been demanding the return of fellow-fighters from Afghanistan in return for the release of the hostages.
The Tajik government flew in 35 fighters from Afghanistan on Friday but the complicated swap was hampered by disagreements over procedure.
The hostages held by Sadirov's men also include three U.N. observers -- two from Switzerland and one from Ukraine -- and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency.

Tajikistan's security minister was also seized last weekend when he tried to negotiate with the hostage-takers, who once backed the former Soviet republic's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.
Questions remained on Saturday about the fate of one of the U.N. observers. Sadirov said on Thursday he had killed an observer, but on Friday he told Ignatenko that the report was untrue.
Russian and Tajik officials negotiated with Sadirov through Friday night and described a tense situation.
"He (Sadirov) is in a very agitated state," Ignatenko told Russian television late on Friday. "His demands are becoming more severe...but we have met them all."
Russia, whose soldiers help police the border with Afghanistan, has appealed for the early release of the captives.
The hostage crisis has highlighted the instability of Tajikistan, an impoverished former Soviet republic bordering Afghanistan and China.
Armed groups opposed to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov are scattered across the country and some fighters, such as those loyal to Sadirov and his brother Rivzon, are based in Afghanistan.
